question: what to do if police arrest me without a warrant
citations: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana, 2025, Division Bench
Kasireddy Upender Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 2025, Division Bench

top_3_cases.title: VIHAAN KUMAR versus STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.
DHANRAJ ASWANI versus AMAR S. MULCHANDANI & ANR.
KASIREDDY UPENDER REDDY versus STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH AND ORS.

ai_answer: If police arrest you without a warrant, you may first demand that they disclose the specific grounds for arrest as required under Section 41(1) CrPC, which permits warrantless arrest only when a cognizable offence is alleged, a reasonable complaint or credible information exists, or a reasonable suspicion is present (Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana, 2025, Division Bench). You should ask to see the arrest memo or diary entry documenting these grounds, and if they cannot produce it, you can invoke your right to bail and challenge the legality of the arrest before a magistrate; the police must also follow the procedural safeguards laid down in the same provision (Kasireddy Upender Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 2025, Division Bench).

question: guidelines for arrest, remand and bail in criminal procedure
citations: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana, 2025, Division Bench
Kasireddy Upender Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 2025, Division Bench
KM. Hema Mishra v. State of U.P., 2014, Division Bench

top_3_cases.title: VIHAAN KUMAR versus STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.
KASIREDDY UPENDER REDDY versus STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH AND ORS.
KM. HEMA MISHRA versus STATE OF U.P. AND OTHERS

ai_answer: Arrest must comply with the procedural safeguards of Article 22(1) of the Constitution; if these are breached, the magistrate must release the accused and may grant bail notwithstanding statutory restrictions (Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana, 2025, Division Bench; Kasireddy Upender Reddy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 2025, Division Bench). When an arrested person is produced before a Judicial Magistrate for remand, the magistrate is duty‑bound to ascertain compliance with Article 22(1), and a violation is a ground for immediate bail (Vihaan Kumar, 2025; Kasireddy Upender Reddy, 2025). Moreover, arrest is not obligatory for every cognizable offence; police must exercise discretion and courts may grant interim bail to prevent irreparable harm to reputation (KM. Hema Mishra v. State of U.P., 2014, Division Bench).

question: compensation for custodial death and police atrocities
citations: Dalbir Singh v. State of U.P. (2009, Division Bench)

ai_answer: Compensation for custodial death is permissible under Article 21, but the court will award it only after the death is conclusively established as occurring in custody, as held in Dalbir Singh v. State of U.P. (2009, Division Bench). The Supreme Court has affirmed that such compensation may be granted to the next of kin and does not preclude further civil or criminal claims, with the quantum determined by the facts of each case, as noted in Sube Singh v. State of Haryana (2006, Division Bench) and reiterated in Re‑Inhuman Conditions in Prisons (2017, Division Bench).

question: remedies for custodial torture and police excesses

ai_answer: The Supreme Court has held that custodial torture violates Article 21 and entitles the victim to monetary compensation for the infringement of fundamental rights, as affirmed in Khurshheed Ahmad Chohan (2025, Division Bench) and Sube Singh (2006, Division Bench). The Court also emphasizes that the State must provide effective remedial mechanisms, including prompt investigation, prosecution of offending officers, and award of compensation to restore dignity, as reflected in the judgments cited.

question: can my landlord evict me without notice
citations: V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal (1979, Constitution Bench)
Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd. (2005, Division Bench)

top_3_cases.title: V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal
VINOD KUMAR versus ASHOK KUMAR GANDHI
Atma Ram Properties (P) Ltd. v. Federal Motors (P) Ltd.

ai_answer: A landlord cannot evict a tenant without observing due process. Where the premises are covered by a State Rent Control Act, the landlord must first establish a statutory ground for eviction and obtain a decree from the competent authority; a contractual notice under Section 106 TPA is not a condition precedent, but eviction cannot be summary or forceful. In non‑rent‑controlled premises, a formal notice under Section 106 is required before filing an eviction petition.

question: tenant protection against unlawful ejectment and eviction under rent control laws
citations: HEERA TRADERS versus KAMLA JAIN (2022, Division Bench)
BHARAT PETROLEUM CORPORATION LIMITED versus R. CHANDRAMOULEESWARAN AND OTHERS (2020, Division Bench)

top_3_cases.title: HEERA TRADERS versus KAMLA JAIN
HARBHAJAN SINGH ETC versus STATE OF PUNJAB AND OTHERS
BHARAT PETROLEUM CORPORATION LIMITED versus R. CHANDRAMOULEESWARAN AND OTHERS

ai_answer: Under the Rent Control Acts, a landlord may seek ejectment only on the grounds enumerated in Section 12, and the tenant enjoys statutory protection against arbitrary eviction; the landlord must serve a proper notice and prove statutory grounds such as default in rent or bona fide personal necessity. The Supreme Court has held that the tenant’s right to occupy is protected by Section 9, which is an equitable privilege that can be invoked to prevent eviction of a tenant who has constructed a superstructure on the demised land. Consequently, any eviction proceeding must comply with the procedural safeguards laid down in the Rent Control Acts and the equitable considerations of Section 9.

question: protection of right to life and personal liberty under Article 21
citations: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (right to privacy) ([2017] 10 S.C.R. 569)

top_3_cases.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (right to privacy)
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India

ai_answer: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017, 9-judge Constitution Bench), the Supreme Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution. The Court affirmed that privacy is intrinsic to life, personal liberty, and freedom of expression, establishing a strict three-fold test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality for any state interference.

question: freedom of speech and reasonable restrictions under Article 19
citations: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978, 7‑judge Constitution Bench
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973, 13‑judge Constitution Bench

top_3_cases.title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (right to privacy)

ai_answer: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression, but the Court has held that this right is subject to reasonable restrictions in the interests of sovereignty, security, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to offence, or any other purpose prescribed by law (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, 1978, 7‑judge Constitution Bench). The doctrine of reasonable restriction is interpreted narrowly to ensure that any law impinging on speech must be proportionate, non‑arbitrary and must satisfy the test of reasonableness as part of the basic structure of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973, 13‑judge Constitution Bench).
